summary:
Burnbook is a web dashboard built on NASA's microgravity combustion research. We have collected these sources into a tool that spacecraft designers and crews can use. Data was pulled from NASA’s Physical Sciences Informatics repository, including BASS, Saffire, ACME, FLEX and CFI test tables and raw sensor files, cleaned with reproducible scripts. 

Users pick a cabin atmosphere, and BurnBook ranks 21 NASA investigations based on similarity in cabin conditions. They can replay real Saffire fires second by second, drag a test point across the ISS flammability boundary to see whether a flame survives, and search 53 claims, each tied to its source and test conditions. An AI assistant answers questions using only those cited claims.

Ground flammability tests are not conservative for microgravity, cabin-wide danger comes from gas rather than heat, and at the oxygen levels planned for exploration vehicles, shutting off ventilation may not put a fire out. With Apollo 1 and 13 as reminders, BurnBook makes this evidence easy to find, check and act on before crews fly.
details:
Burnbook is a web dashboard built on NASA's microgravity combustion research. We have collected these sources into a tool that spacecraft designers and crews can use. Data was pulled from NASA’s Physical Sciences Informatics repository, including BASS, Saffire, ACME, FLEX and CFI test tables and raw sensor files, cleaned with reproducible scripts.

The primary benifit of the project is that it consolidates numerous different sources into one single, searchable source. This reduces the friction of research and lets non specialist -such as mission planners, students or designers - ask questions in plain english and still get answers backed by research and data.

NASA plans exploration vehicles with up to 34% oxygen at reduced pressure. BurnBook brings relevant evidence:

  • Ground flammability tests are not conservative for microgravity.
  • In large orbital fires, the cabin-wide danger was gas rather than heat.
  • At elevated oxygen, cutting ventilation may not put a flame out.

We want designers, mission planners and students to be able to access this information, where they can then find gaps in data that new expirements need to fill.

Tools and technologies

  • Languages: Python for data processing and the API (Starlette, uvicorn, numpy, openpyxl); HTML, CSS and plain JavaScript for the interface
  • Language models: a provider-independent layer that supports Google Gemini, Anthropic, and any OpenAI-compatible service, with automatic fallback.
  • Testing and checks: 34 pytest tests; Playwright screenshots at phone, desktop and dark-mode settings.
  • Hosting and source control: Render for hosting; GitHub for the code.
  • AI assistance: We used an AI coding assistant (Claude) for consolidation of research and data processing, fact checking, and testing scripts.
  • Hardware: none beyond our laptops.
